'''''Salvia hispanica''''', one of several related species commonly known as '''chia''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|tʃ|iː|ə}}), is a species of flowering plant in the [[Mentha|mint]] family, [[Lamiaceae]]. It is native to central and southern Mexico and [[Guatemala]]. It is considered a [[pseudocereal]], cultivated for its edible, [[Hydrophile|hydrophilic]] [[chia seed]], grown and commonly used as food in several countries of western [[South America]], western Mexico, and the [[southwestern United States]].

==Description==
Chia is an [[annual plant|annual]] herb growing up to {{convert|1.75|m|ftin|abbr=off}} tall, with [[Phyllotaxis|opposite]] [[leaves]] that are {{convert|4|–|8|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|3|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide. Its flowers are purple or white and are produced in numerous clusters in a [[Raceme|spike]] at the end of each stem.<ref name="Sahagun">Anderson, A.{{nbsp}}J.{{nbsp}}O. and Dibble, C.{{nbsp}}E. "An Ethnobiography of the Nahuatl", The [[Florentine Codex]], (translation of the work by Fr.{{nbsp}}[[Bernardino de Sahagún]]), Books 10–11, from the Period 1558–1569</ref>
[[File:Chia plant leafs.jpg|thumb|Chia leaves]]
Typically, the seeds are small ovals with a diameter around {{convert|1|mm|in|abbr=on|frac=32}}. They are mottle-colored, with brown, gray, black, and white. The seeds are hydrophilic, absorbing up to 12 times their weight in liquid when soaked. While soaking, the seeds develop a [[mucilaginous]] coating that gives chia-based beverages a distinctive [[gel]]atinous texture.<ref>Muñoz, Loreto A.; Cobos, Angel; Diaz, Olga; Aguilera, José Miguel (2013). "Chia Seed (Salvia hispanica): An Ancient Grain and a New Functional Food". ''Food Reviews International''. '''29''' (4): 394–408. doi:10.1080/87559129.2013.818014.</ref>

Many plants cultivated as ''S.{{nbsp}}hispanica'' are in fact [[Salvia officinalis subsp. lavandulifolia|''S. officinalis'' subsp. ''lavandulifolia'']] (syn. ''S. lavandulifolia'').<ref>Mark Griffiths, Editor. ''Index of Garden Plants.'' (Portland, Oregon: [[Timber Press]], 2nd American Edition, 1995.) {{ISBN|0-88192-246-3}}.</ref>

== Etymology ==
The word ''chia'' is derived from the [[Nahuatl]] word {{lang|nci|chian}}, meaning 'oily'.{{ref label|Sahagun69|1|a}}

Other plants known as ''chia'' include ''[[Salvia columbariae]]'',<ref name="usda03">{{cite web |author=Immel, Diana L |date=29 January 2003 |title=Chia, ''Salvia columbariae'' Benth.; Plant Symbol = SACO6 |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/cs_saco6.pdf |access-date=27 May 2017 |publisher=Natural Resources Conservation Service, US Department of Agriculture}}</ref> which is sometimes called "golden chia",{{Cn|date=June 2021}} ''[[Salvia polystachia]]'', and ''[[Salvia tiliifolia]]''.

== Distribution and habitat ==
Chia is native to central and southern Mexico and [[Guatemala]].<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN|access-date=21 March 2012}}</ref> It is hardy from [[Hardiness zone|USDA Zones]] 9–12.

== Cultivation ==
{{main|Chia seed}}

Chia is grown and consumed commercially in its native Mexico and Guatemala, as well as Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, [[Nicaragua]], northwestern Argentina, parts of Australia, and the southwestern United States.<ref name="usda03" /><ref>{{cite web |author=Dunn C |date=25 May 2015 |title=Is chia the next quinoa? |url=http://www.smh.com.au/small-business/growing/is-chia-the-next-quinoa-20150514-gh1mb2.html |access-date=13 February 2016 |publisher=The Sydney Morning Herald}}</ref> New patented varieties of chia have been bred in Kentucky for cultivation in northern latitudes of the United States.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Cheryl Kaiser |author2=Matt Ernst |date=February 2016 |title=Chia |url=https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CCD/introsheets/chia.pdf |access-date=13 February 2016 |publisher=University of Kentucky, College of Agriculture, Food and Environment, Center for Crop Diversification Crop Profile |archive-date=15 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170115104605/https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CCD/introsheets/chia.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

It is grown commercially for its [[seed]], a food rich in [[omega-3 fatty acid]]s since the seeds yield 25–30% extractable [[Vegetable fats and oils|oil]], including [[Alpha-linolenic acid|α-linolenic acid]]. Typical composition of the fat of the oil is 55% [[omega-3 fatty acid|ω-3]], 18% [[omega-6 fatty acid|ω-6]], 6% [[omega-9 fatty acid|ω-9]], and 10% [[saturated fat]].<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |year=2010 |title=Nutrition facts for dried chia seeds, one ounce |url=http://nutritiondata.self.com/facts/nut-and-seed-products/3061/2 |publisher=Conde Nast for the USDA National Nutrient Database, SR-21}}</ref>

===Climate and growing cycle length===
The length of the growing cycle for chia varies based on location and is influenced by [[elevation]].<ref name="ayerza_coates2009">{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1016/j.indcrop.2009.03.009
| issn = 0926-6690
| volume = 30
| issue = 2
| pages = 321–324
| last = Ayerza (h)
| first = Ricardo
|author2=Wayne Coates
| title = Influence of environment on growing period and yield, protein, oil and α-linolenic content of three chia (Salvia hispanica L.) selections
| journal = Industrial Crops and Products
| year = 2009
}}</ref> For production sites located in different ecosystems in Bolivia, Ecuador and northwestern Argentina, growing cycles are between 100 and 150 days in duration.<ref name="ayerza2009">{{Cite journal
| volume = 58
| issue = 7
| pages = 347–354
| last = Ayerza
| first = Ricardo
| title = The Seed's Protein and Oil Content, Fatty Acid Composition, and Growing Cycle Length of a Single Genotype of Chia (''Salvia hispanica'' L.) as Affected by Environmental Factors
| journal = Journal of Oleo Science
| year = 2009
| doi=10.5650/jos.58.347
| pmid = 19491529
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Accordingly, commercial production fields are located in the range of {{convert|8|–|2200|m|ft|abbr=on}} altitude across a variety of [[ecosystem]]s ranging from tropical [[coastal desert]], to [[tropical rain forest]], and inter-[[Andean]] dry valley.<ref name="ayerza2009" /> In northwestern Argentina, a time span from planting to harvest of 120–180 days is reported for fields located at elevations of {{convert|900|–|1500|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name="ayerza1998">{{Cite journal
| volume = 75
| issue = 10
| pages = 1417–1420
| last1 = Coates
| first1 = Wayne
| first2 = Ricardo |last2=Ayerza
| title = Commercial production of chia in Northwestern Argentina
| journal = Journal of the American Oil Chemists' Society
| date = 1998
| doi=10.1007/s11746-998-0192-7
| s2cid = 95974159
}}</ref>
[[File:Chia seed.jpg|thumb|An extreme macro photograph of a chia seed]]
''S. hispanica'' is a short-day flowering plant,<ref name="jamboonsri">{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1007/s10722-011-9673-x
| volume = 59
| issue = 2
| pages = 171–178
| last = Jamboonsri
| first = Watchareewan
|author2=Timothy D. Phillips |author3=Robert L. Geneve |author4=Joseph P. Cahill |author5=David F. Hildebrand
 | title = Extending the range of an ancient crop, Salvia hispanica L.—a new ω3 source
| journal = Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution
| year = 2012
| s2cid = 14751137
}}</ref> indicating its [[photoperiodic]] sensitivity and lack of photoperiodic variability in traditional cultivars, which limited commercial use of chia seeds to tropical and subtropical latitudes until 2012.<ref name="university_kentucky2012">{{Cite conference
| publisher = Cooperative Extension Service. University of Kentucky – College of Agriculture
| title = Chia
| access-date = 2014-11-18
| year = 2012
| url = http://www.uky.edu/Ag/CCD/introsheets/chia.pdf
}}</ref> Now, traditional domesticated lines of ''Salvia'' species grow naturally or can be cultivated in [[temperate]] zones at higher latitudes in the United States.<ref name=usda03/><ref name="jamboonsri" /> In [[Arizona]] and [[Kentucky]], seed maturation of traditional chia cultivars is stopped by [[frost]] before or after flower set, preventing seed harvesting.<ref name="jamboonsri" /> Advances in [[plant breeding]] during 2012, however, led to development of new early-flowering chia [[genotype]]s proving to have higher yields in Kentucky.<ref name="university_kentucky2012" />

===Seed yield and composition===
Seed yield varies depending on [[cultivar]]s, mode of cultivation, and growing conditions by geographic region. For example, commercial fields in Argentina and Colombia vary in yield range from {{convert|450|to|1250|kg/ha|lb/acre}}.<ref name="ayerza1998" /><ref name="coates_ayerza1996" /> A small-scale study with three cultivars grown in the inter-Andean valleys of Ecuador produced yields up to {{convert|2300|kg/ha|lb/acre|abbr=on}}, indicating that the favorable growing environment and cultivar interacted to produce the high yields.<ref name="ayerza_coates2009" /> Genotype has a larger effect on yield than on protein content, oil content, fatty acid composition, or phenolic compounds, whereas high temperature reduces oil content and degree of unsaturation, and raises protein content.{{Citation needed|date=December 2019|reason=removed citation to predatory publisher content}}

=== Soil, seedbed requirements, and sowing===
The cultivation of ''S. hispanica'' requires light to medium clay or sandy soils.<ref name="munoz2013">{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.1080/87559129.2013.818014
| volume = 29
| issue = 4
| pages = 394–408
| last = Muñoz
| first = Loreto A.
|author2=Angel Cobos |author3=Olga Diaz |author4=José Miguel Aguilera
 | title = Chia Seed ( ''Salvia hispanica'' ): An Ancient Grain and a New Functional Food
| journal = Food Reviews International
| year = 2013
| s2cid = 85052922
}}</ref> The plant prefers well-drained, moderately fertile soils, but can cope with acid soils and moderate drought.<ref name="university_kentucky2012" /><ref name="munoz2013" /> Sown chia seeds need moisture for seedling establishment, while the maturing chia plant does not tolerate wet soils during growth.<ref name="university_kentucky2012" />

Traditional cultivation techniques of ''S. hispanica'' include soil preparation by disruption and loosening followed by seed broadcasting.<ref name="cahill2005">{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.2993/0278-0771(2005)25[155:HSADOC]2.0.CO;2
| issn = 0278-0771
| volume = 25
| issue = 2
| pages = 155–174
| last = Cahill
| first = Joseph P.
| title = Human Selection and Domestication of Chia (''Salvia hispanica'' L.)
| journal = Journal of Ethnobiology
| year = 2005
| s2cid = 85924063
}}</ref> In modern commercial production, a typical sowing rate of {{convert|6|kg/ha|lb/acre|abbr=on}} and row spacing of {{convert|0.7–0.8|m|abbr=on}} are usually applied.<ref name="ayerza1998" />

=== Fertilization and irrigation===
''S. hispanica'' can be cultivated under low fertilizer input, using {{convert|100|kg/ha|lb/acre|abbr=on}} nitrogen or in some cases, no fertilizer is used.<ref name="jamboonsri" /><ref name="coates_ayerza1996">{{Cite journal
| volume = 5
| issue = 3
| pages = 229–233
| last = Coates
| first = Wayne
|author2=Ricardo Ayerza
| title = Production potential of chia in northwestern Argentina
| journal = Industrial Crops and Products
| year = 1996
| doi=10.1016/0926-6690(96)89454-4
}}</ref>

Irrigation frequency in chia production fields may vary from none to eight irrigations per growing season, depending on climatic conditions and rainfall.<ref name="coates_ayerza1996" />

===Genetic diversity and breeding===
The wide range of wild and cultivated varieties of ''S. hispanica'' are based on seed size, [[shattering (agriculture)|shattering]] of seeds, and seed color.<ref name="Cahill 2005">Cahill, J. P. and B. Ehdaie (2005). "Variation and heritability of seed mass in chia (''Salvia hispanica'' L.)." Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution 52(2): 201-207. [[doi:10.1007/s10722-003-5122-9]]. Retrieved 2014-11-29</ref><ref name="Cahill 2002">{{cite journal|vauthors=Cahill JP, Provance, MC |year=2002|title=Genetics of qualitative traits in domesticated chia (Salvia hispanica L.)|journal=Journal of Heredity|volume=93|issue=1|pages=52–55|pmid=12011177|doi=10.1093/jhered/93.1.52|doi-access=free}}</ref> Seed weight and color have high [[heritability]], with a single [[recessive gene]] responsible for white color.<ref name="Cahill 2002" />

===Diseases and crop management===
Currently, no major pests or diseases affect chia production.<ref name="munoz2013" /> [[Essential oil]]s in chia leaves have repellent properties against insects, making it suitable for organic cultivation.<ref name="university_kentucky2012" /> Virus infections, however, possibly transmitted by white flies, may occur.<ref name=celli2014>{{Cite journal
| doi = 10.3390/v6093450
| pmid = 25243369
| pmc = 4189032
| issn = 1999-4915
| volume = 6
| issue = 9
| pages = 3450–3457
| last = Celli
| first = Marcos
|author2=Maria Perotto |author3=Julia Martino |author4=Ceferino Flores |author5=Vilma Conci |author6=Patricia Pardina
 | title = Detection and Identification of the First Viruses in Chia (''Salvia hispanica'')
| journal = Viruses
| date = 2014
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Weeds may present a problem in the early development of the chia crop until its canopy closes, but because chia is sensitive to most commonly used [[herbicides]], mechanical weed control is preferred.<ref name="university_kentucky2012" />

==Nutrition==
{{Main|Chia seed#Nutrition}}
Dried chia seeds are 6% water, 42% [[carbohydrate]]s, 17% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and 31% [[fat]] (table). In a reference amount of {{convert|100|g}}, chia seeds supply 486 [[calorie]]s and are a rich source (20% or more of the [[Daily Value]], DV) of several [[B vitamins]] and [[mineral (nutrient)|dietary minerals]] (table).
